ingredients.item: soybean sprouts , rinsed, loose hulls and sad stragglers picked out
ingredients.preparation: kongnamul, the yellow-beaned ones — mung sprouts are a different, softer thing

ingredients.item: Water to barely cover , 1 tsp salt
A pinch of gochugaru , optional color
fish sauce or soy sauce , optional depth

instructions.heading: Step 1
instructions.action: Salted water at a full boil, sprouts in, uncovered — the law of this record. Six minutes at a steady boil, stirred once.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: a test sprout: the tail is fully tender (no string) and the bean is just soft with the faintest bite, and the raw-grassy smell from the pot's first minute has cooked off entirely — that smell leaving is exactly what the uncovered boil lets happen.

instructions.heading: Step 2
instructions.action: Drain well — really well, a full minute in the colander, shaking — and turn the hot sprouts into the seasoning bowl while they still steam.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the residual heat is doing the garlic's cooking: thirty seconds after tossing, the bowl smells nutty-savory, not sharp-raw.

instructions.heading: Step 3
instructions.action: Toss with everything, taste, adjust — the banchan should read sesame-first, salt behind, a clean crunch.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the eating test with rice and any grilled meat from this site's M-list: the sprouts reset the palate between rich bites. That is the banchan's job description, and this bowl does it as well as anything on the table.

storageNotes: Keeps 2–3 days refrigerated and holds crunch better than most banchan; refresh with a few drops of sesame oil at serving.
Variations: a spoon of gochugaru for the red build; the spinach (#B06) and bellflower (#B17) records run this same blanch-and-dress pattern; day-after sprouts folded into bibimbap or fried rice.
